name: wide (f32x4/f32x8 SIMD types, measured through ultraviolet and nalgebra/simba AoSoA types)
baseline: Scalar per-element math with glam 0.34.1 (one Vec3/Mat4 at a time) doing the same total work
verdict_reason: Rewriting math in structure-of-arrays form on wide-backed f32x8 types gives 3.9x to 12.4x more throughput than one-at-a-time glam, but only after restructuring data and algorithms, and all published numbers use target-cpu=native (f32x8 needs AVX2). Some operations, such as 4x4 transpose, get slower.
tier_reason: mathbench is public, and the README states the rustc version, RUSTFLAGS, CPU and library versions.
claimed_speedup: ns per element, glam_f32x1 vs ultraviolet_f32x8: ray-sphere intersection 9.2936 vs 0.7473, vector3 length 1.2698 vs 0.1621, matrix4 inverse 11.0112 vs 2.8535, matrix4 mul matrix4 3.1637 vs 2.5313 (12.4x, 7.8x, 3.9x, 1.25x) (derived from page data). ultraviolet_f32x4: ray-sphere 1.2298, vector3 length 0.3208 ns (7.6x, 4.0x) (derived from page data). Slower: matrix4 transpose 1.4185 vs 2.4720 ns
workload: mathbench "wide" benchmarks: AoSoA (array of structs of arrays) versions of vector, matrix, rotation and ray-sphere operations over 16 to 80,000 elements, compared with scalar glam doing the same total work; time per element.
toolchain: rustc 1.99.0 (b940084d7 2026-09-28), default bench profile plus RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native'
platforms: x86/x86_64 (SSE2 baseline, AVX/AVX2 when enabled at build time), aarch64 NEON, wasm32 simd128, scalar fallback elsewhere; stable Rust
one_liner: Stable-Rust SIMD vector types; AoSoA math built on them runs 4-12x faster than one-at-a-time glam in mathbench, with target-cpu=native.
how_it_is_fast: wide provides f32x4, f32x8 and integer lane types that map to SSE, AVX or NEON registers selected at compile time. Libraries such as ultraviolet and simba store 4 or 8 vectors per struct, one lane per vector, so each instruction processes 4 or 8 independent elements instead of one.
use_it_when: You process many independent vectors or rays (particles, physics, ray tracing) and can lay data out as structure-of-arrays.
You need explicit SIMD on stable Rust without writing per-architecture intrinsics.
skip_it_when: Your algorithm works on one vector at a time or needs horizontal operations; transposes measured slower.
You ship generic x86_64 binaries: f32x8 falls back to two 128-bit halves without AVX2 enabled at build time, and wide does no runtime dispatch.
caveats: All numbers use target-cpu=native on a Ryzen 7 3800X; mathbench notes that the f32x8 benchmarks require AVX2.
The benchmark measures wide through ultraviolet 0.10.0 (which depends on wide 0.7) and nalgebra's simba types, not wide directly, and against a baseline that already uses SSE2 per vector.
mathbench itself warns that scalar and wide results are not a direct comparison because the algorithms are restructured.
tradeoffs: Requires restructuring data into AoSoA form and rewriting branches as lane masks.
Instruction set is fixed at compile time; no runtime feature detection.

evidence.quote: | ray-sphere intersection x80000 |    9.2936 ns   |           1.2298 ns   |        1.2658 ns   |         __0.7473 ns__ |        0.7690 ns   |
RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo bench --features wide wide
Note that the `nalgebra` wide benchmarks use `simba`'s stable, `wide` crate backed types (`WideF32x4` and `WideF32x8`), so they build on stable Rust.
Additionally the `f32x8` benchmarks will require the `AVX2` instruction set
